knowledgePattern: Check strict integer bounds before using factorial factors
solution:
Lines 1–6 are valid. In the unequal-factor case, both factors are distinct integers in (n−1)!, so their product n divides that factorial. In the square case, n=a2 with a≥2.

Line 7 claims 2a<a2 for every a≥2. It fails at a=2, where both sides equal 4. Thus the factor 2a need not appear in (n−1)!.

The statement itself is false: n=4 divides none of 1!=1,2!=2,3!=6, but is not prime. The first error is line 7, option G.

hints.title: Check that the proposed factors really occur
hints.body: When a proof uses factors from a factorial, verify that each factor lies within the factorial’s stated integer range.
hints.recap: Divisibility requires actual integer factors; endpoint restrictions cannot be omitted.
hints.pitfall: A factor equal to n is not included in (n−1)!.
hints.pause: Audit the distinct-factor and equal-factor cases separately.
